name: Nyiha
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 7 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Kashoki, Mubanga E. & Michael Mann. 1978. A general sketch of the Bantu languages of Zambia. In Sirarpi Ohannessian & Mubanga E. Kashoki (eds.), Language in Zambia, 47-100. London: International African Institute. (of the open UNZA DSpace scan,https://dspace.unza.zm/server/api/core/bitstreams/9c70f9aa-7369-4b1f-9394-567a7f81d5c0/content)
catalog_locator: Ch. 2, sec. 3.4 'Tone and Stress', pp. 70-71 (on-disk; excerpt). Scope sentence p. 62; penultimate-lengthening rule pp. 63-64; per-language hedge p. 64; Nyiha among the 25 sampled varieties, Table 2:1; Nyiha located in Isoka and Chama Districts (Ch. 1, p. 14).
catalog_quote: In Zambian languages, in contrast, syllables are more or less evenly stressed, i.e. they are pronounced with almost the same degree of prominence or force. In some languages, however, (e.g. Cewa) the penultimate syllable seems to be pronounced with slightly greater force than the rest of the syllables in the same word. However, it must be remembered that that is also the syllable, according to the rule mentioned earlier, which is lengthened, so that the stress may be the effect of the lengthening of the vowel. In any case, independent of the lengthening of vowels, stress in Zambian languages does not distinguish words from each other in meaning. A characteristic feature of all Zambian languages is that each of their syllables carries tone. ... There are only two contrastive tones in Zambian languages, high and low, which serve to distinguish ... between words which are otherwise identical in all other respects.
world_status: statement found in a copy we already had

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: QUOTE: Found at the stated locator in lines 3184-3194 (Kashoki & Mann 1978, ch. 2 sec. 3.4 'Tone and Stress', p. 70; excerpt also; Verbatim apart from scanned artefacts the compiler normalised ('hovvever', 'syilable', 'vvhich', 'vovvel', 'vvords'). Context checked: scope sentence p. 62 (lines 2802-2809: 'concerned only with patterns common among all Zambian languages as illustrated by the languages which we studied'); penultimate-lengthening rule pp. 63-64 (lines 2872-2879) asserted only for Eastern Province and several North-Western Province languages; per-language hedge p. 64 (lines 2893-2895); 'Nyiha' is one of the 25 sampled varieties (Table 2:1, line 2466; wordlist columns pp. 82-83) a…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Areal generalisation over the authors' 25-variety Zambian sample (which includes 'Nyiha' of Isoka/Chama = nkv): no contrastive word stress; syllables roughly evenly prominent; where a penult sounds stronger (e.g. Cewa) it is attributed to automatic penultimate vowel lengthening. Nothing is asserted about Nyiha/Nyika individually, and penultimate lengthening itself is asserted only for Eastern-Province and some North-Western-Province languages.
new_statements.exceptions: Cewa (and by implication other penult-lengthening languages) may show slight penultimate prominence; authors caution that 'all these phonetic details have to be studied.. for each individual language' (p. 64).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level, impressionistic, areal; not a language-specific description of Nyika. Every stress remark is tied to tone (two tones, H/L, on every syllable) and to phrase/word-penultimate lengthening. Treat as an overview placeholder, not a primary statement for nkv.
new_statements.identity_note: nkv (nyik1246) = Chinyika of Chisenga (Chitipa District, Malawi) and Mulekatembo (Isoka District, Zambia), c. 10,000 speakers, created by ISO CR 2007-047 on the basis of the 2004 SIL survey; distinct from Nyiha (Malawi) [nyr, nyih1239 = Kameme variety], Nyiha (Tanzania) [nih, nyih1240, Mbozi/Mbeya: Busse 1943, Yukawa 1989] and Nyika (Tanzania) [nkt]. The quoted Kashoki & Mann 1978 statement is an areal generalisation over Zambian Bantu; their sampled 'Nyiha' is the Isoka/Chama (Zambia) variety, which Glottolog codes as nkv. Malawian 'Cinyika' in Chiona 2005 / Mtenje 2007 may denote either Chisenga Nyika (nkv) or Kameme Nyiha (nyr): CLS 2006 treats 'Cinyiha/Cinyika' as a single language group; Glottolog's tagging of those two works to nkv is auto-translated from Maho's M23 code, not a variety identification. Yukawa 1989 (downloaded) describes nih, not nkv.

sources.citation: Mtenje, Atikonda A. 2016. A comparative analysis of the phonology and morpho-syntax of Cisukwa, Cindali and Cilambya. PhD thesis, University of Cape Town.
sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request); access check: not located online or in the libraries checked
sources.note: Describes the neighbouring SuNdaLa cluster (Cisukwa/Cindali/Cilambya = ndal1241/lamb1272), not Nyika: verbs are 'accentual' with H on the penultimate (or antepenultimate) mora and pre-pausal penultimate vowel lengthening (pp. 27, ch. 4). Mentions Cinyika only to list it among Chitipa languages (CLS 2006 language group 3 'Cinyiha/Cinyika') and to characterise Chiona 2005 as an unpublished undergraduate dissertation on syllable structure/hiatus resolution in Cindali compared with Cinyika. No stress statement for Nyika.

sources.citation: Mtenje, Al. 2011. On relative clauses and prosodic phrasing in Ciwandya. ZAS Papers in Linguistics 55: 121-146.
sources.note: Ciwandya of Chitipa (Wanda/Wandya, not nkv): long penultimate vowels with falling tones mark right edges of phonological phrases. Nothing on Nyika.

sources.citation: Glottolog 5.1 CLDF sources.bib (24 entries tagged [nkv]); Hyman 2009 (penultimate lengthening) and Botne 1998 (Chindali) texts held under ndal1241
sources.note: No grammar or phonology of Malawi/Zambia Nyika exists in Glottolog's list (items are Tanzanian Nyiha: Busse 1943, Yukawa 1989, texts; ethnography; the SIL survey; Kashoki & Mann 1978; Chiona 2005; Mtenje 2007). Hyman 2009 and Botne 1998 do not mention Nyika/Nyiha.

sources.note: The only work devoted to Malawi/Zambia Nyika (Chisenga, Mulekatembo) as distinct from Tanzanian Nyiha; contains wordlists and linguistic comparison; may carry brief phonological notes and settles which 'Cinyika' is which.
